segments.say: We've looked at the pull of the feed, the reward of a like, the habit of comparison, the cost of interruption, the spread of stories, and the toll on sleep. Now the practical question. What can a person do about it, tomorrow morning, that the evidence actually supports? The good news is that the answers are modest, and doable.

The most important idea in this chapter is that the answer isn't mainly about willpower. The research on habits and self-control suggests that people who do well don't resist temptation harder. They arrange their lives so that there's less to resist. That's a more hopeful message, because design can be changed in minutes.

Wendy Wood and her colleagues asked people to keep diaries of what they did, at random times during the day. They found that about forty-three percent of everyday actions were performed almost daily in the same context, and often while thinking about something else. A large part of what we do is habit, set off by place, time and cue, more than by a decision.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2002
show.what: Habits in everyday life: thought, emotion, and action

segments.say: If so much of life is habit, then the cue matters. A phone on the bedside table is a cue. A notification is a cue. The sofa after dinner is a cue. Change the cue, and you change the habit more reliably than by a good intention. This is the foundation for the first few tools.

show.title: Everyday actions that were habitual
show.label: in a diary study, performed almost daily in the same setting

segments.say: The first tool is friction, which we met at the start of the evening. Add a little effort to the things you want to do less. Log out of the apps after each use. Move them off the home screen. Keep the phone in another room while you work, or while you sleep. None of this is dramatic, and each step takes only a minute.
The evidence for each is partly indirect, from the work on habits, attention and sleep we've seen. But the logic is consistent, and many people find a noticeable difference within days.

show.title: Friction you can add
items: Remove the apps from your home screen
Log out after each session
Charge the phone outside the bedroom
Turn off non-essential notifications
Use a plain alarm clock

segments.say: The second tool is a plan. In 2006, Peter Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran reviewed ninety-four studies of a technique called implementation intentions. The idea is to turn a vague goal into an if-then plan: if this situation happens, then I'll do this specific thing.

Across ninety-four independent tests, people who made if-then plans were considerably more likely to reach their goals than those who only set an intention, with a medium-to-large effect. The plan seems to hand control of the action to the situation, so that you don't have to decide in the moment, when you're tired or tempted.

show.what: Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis of effects and processes

segments.say: Plans like these are simple, specific and kind to yourself. They don't rely on an iron will. They give your future, slightly tired self a script to follow.

show.title: If-then plans for the feed
items: If I feel the urge to check, then I'll take three slow breaths first
If it's after ten at night, then the phone goes in the kitchen
If I open the app without a reason, then I'll close it and stretch
If I want to share something, then I'll wait a minute first

segments.say: The third tool comes from the experiments we saw earlier. Hunt's team found that limiting use to ten minutes per platform helped students feel less lonely and less depressed. Allcott's team found that four weeks without Facebook brought small improvements in mood and more time with family and friends. Neither is a miracle, but both were real.

show.title: Tool three: set limits and take breaks

segments.say: You don't need to commit to a lifelong change. Try a two-week limit, or a weekend off, and notice what changes. Keep a note of your mood, your sleep and your time. If you feel better, you've learned something about your own life that no study could tell you. If you don't, you've lost nothing.

When you slip, which you will, the research on habits suggests that a single slip makes little difference. It's the way you talk to yourself afterwards that counts. Harsh self-criticism tends to make people give up. A calm, curious response, such as noticing what led to the slip, is more likely to help you try again.

The fourth tool is about what you see. The studies of comparison and contagion suggest that who you follow matters. Mute accounts that leave you feeling small. Follow people who teach you things or make you laugh. And make a habit of reaching out to the people who matter, since active, personal use was the kind most linked to wellbeing.
These are cheap and quick, and they work in the direction that the evidence points. They don't promise that your feed will be perfect. They shift the balance a little, day after day.

show.title: Shaping the feed
items: Mute or unfollow accounts that leave you drained
Follow people you can learn from
Send one real message a day
Pause before you share anything that stirs strong emotion

segments.say: A calm morning, a notebook, and a phone left face down by the window. This is what all of the research tends to point towards: not an escape from technology, but a life arranged so that the technology serves you, and the people and things that matter come first.

If all of this feels like a lot, here is a week to try. On the first day, turn off notifications you don't need. On the third, move the phone's charger out of the bedroom. On the fifth, write one if-then plan for a moment when you tend to scroll. And on the seventh, look back, and decide what to keep. It's gentle on purpose. The research on habits suggests that small, specific and repeatable changes outlast big dramatic ones, and that they leave you in charge.

show.title: Your first week
items: Day one: turn off non-essential notifications
Day three: charge the phone outside the bedroom
Day five: make one if-then plan
Day seven: review what changed and keep what helped

segments.say: Four terms from this final chapter. An implementation intention is an if-then plan. A habit cue is a trigger that sets off a routine. Friction is the effort that stands between you and an action. And self-monitoring means observing your own behaviour, which is the first step to changing it.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter
items: Implementation intention
Habit cue
Friction
Self-monitoring

segments.say: After sixteen chapters, here is a fair summary. Social media isn't a poison and it isn't a cure. It's a powerful set of tools built on old human instincts: for rewards, for belonging, for comparison, for news. It can feed us or drain us, depending on how it's built and how we use it, and that gives us more power than the headlines suggest.

You are allowed to put the phone down and look out of the window. You are allowed to be unreachable for an hour. And you're allowed to use these tools with pleasure and without guilt, for the things that they do well. What the evidence asks is only that you stay awake while you do it.

show.sub: You are allowed to log off

segments.say: So what did we learn? That feeds pull on very old systems of reward, belonging and comparison. That the average harm in large studies is small, though not for everyone. That attention, sleep and relationships are the places where it matters most. And that small changes in design and habit beat willpower.

show.sub: What the whole evening taught us

segments.say: Thank you for spending this time. Put the phone somewhere out of reach, let the light go low, and sleep well. Next time, we'll turn to a different kind of difficulty: the conversations that feel impossible, with the people closest to us, and what the research says about listening, disagreeing and still staying connected.
